# Bootstrapping an AI-Native Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The more designers involved in using the new methods, and the better they are able to communicate with each other, the faster the process of cultural integration runs."
>
> — Lynn Conway, *The MPC Adventures* [@Conway1981MPCAdventures, p. 2]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What must exist beyond any one team for AI-native architecture claims to become comparable, and how much of it can a single team adopt without waiting?*

**Core thesis:** *Scaling AI-native architecture requires shared community infrastructure (open process data, neutral benchmark governance, and shared verification access), complemented by immediate unilateral adoption of rigorous reporting and matched baselines.*
:::

An architecture team can retain failed runs, measure its costs, and improve its comparisons without waiting for the discipline to agree on a standard. It cannot make another team's tool interpret a record correctly, establish a neutral public benchmark, or provide its own access to a fabrication process through better recordkeeping alone. Those limits require coordination. This chapter separates local practices from proposals for shared interfaces, implementation access, evaluation, and education (@fig-ch12-cover-map). The proposals connect limits encountered earlier in the book to work the community could undertake; their adoption and effectiveness remain to be established.

![**Separating local practice from shared community coordination.** Individual design teams can immediately adopt rigorous local practices, including lineage tracking, negative-result retention, and matched baselines. Broader claims spanning cross-organizational exchange, neutral benchmarks, and fabrication access depend on shared community infrastructure.](images/ch12-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch12-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which one team can improve records and comparisons now, while cross-team, physical or silicon, and public-program claims require different shared infrastructure."}

## Ecosystem Workstreams and Dependencies {#sec-staging-sequence}

In autumn 1979, Lynn Conway ignited a democratization breakthrough in computer architecture: the ARPANET-enabled Multi-Project Chip (MPC79) run[^fn-mpc79-mosis-c12] [@MeadConway1980VLSI; @Conway1981MPCAdventures]. Conway recognized that custom silicon was throttled because circuit layout remained chained to the proprietary, bespoke fabrication rules of individual foundries. Conway formulated scalable, dimensionless design rules ($\lambda$-rules) that decoupled logical architecture from semiconductor manufacturing physics, while Xerox PARC aggregated layout files transmitted by university students over ARPANET email for photolithographic merging. That workflow shattered the capital barrier to physical silicon. Dozens of academic microarchitectures were fabricated on shared Hewlett-Packard wafers in weeks. The subsequent DARPA-funded MOSIS broker service institutionalized this multi-project wafer model, catalyzing four decades of university very-large-scale integration (VLSI) exploration [@MOSIS1981VLSI].

Today, AI-native computer architecture faces an equivalent democratization crisis. Machine learning generators and automated optimizers can synthesize thousands of candidate microarchitectures an hour. Yet empirical validation remains trapped behind million-dollar commercial electronic design automation (EDA) tool licenses, proprietary foundry non-disclosure agreements, and fifty-million-dollar leading-edge mask sets. Architecture 2.0 requires an equivalent Conway leap: open data schemas, machine-verifiable tool contracts, reproducible multi-project shuttles, and shared failure repositories that turn speculative algorithmic proposals into qualified, physical silicon evidence. The ownership boundaries of @sec-what-architect-owns remain absolute, but the empirical infrastructure required to sustain them must become shared community commons.

Deploying closed-loop search without shared interfaces risks compounding fragmentation in EDA. A learned placer may depend on features specific to a tool version, standard-cell library, or process deck. Within that environment, the dependency can remain implicit; transferring the method exposes it. The operational layers of @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration describe the scope of automated work, but none guarantees interoperability. A system that must carry a design across tools and organizations also needs explicit agreements about those dependencies.

Six proposals address different parts of that coordination problem. For each one, @tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence separates what a team can start inside its own repositories from what requires shared infrastructure, and identifies the earlier limit or risk that motivates the proposal.

| **Proposal** | **Ecosystem action** | **Local starting point** | **Coordination dependency** | **Earlier limit or risk** |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Shared data schemas and tool contracts | Retain decision context, artifact identities, commands, returns, failures, and costs in a versioned record. | Cross-team comparison needs common semantics for identities, status, units, and tool results. | Tool-specific wrappers and limits on model transfer across tool flows (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). |
| 2 | Open implementation paths and cloud silicon shuttles | Exercise an open flow at a named manufacturable or predictive node and state the resulting evidence boundary. | Silicon claims need a manufacturable process design kit (PDK), an accepted fabrication path, and device measurements; commercial-node signoff needs foundry-qualified decks, libraries, tools, and access. | Physical timing, power-delivery, and thermal checks left unmeasured (@sec-what-architect-owns). |
| 3 | Consortium governance and matched benchmarks | Run a matched local comparison with pinned tasks, checks, budgets, and total-cost accounting. | A public leaderboard needs neutral rules, shared task versions, audit capacity, and comparator governance. | Benchmark-health and matched-baseline risks (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| 4 | Grand challenges and architecture contests | Run a narrow evaluator-owned challenge with a credible baseline and explicit untested conditions. | Cross-organization contests depend on stable interfaces, comparable checks, and enforceable resource accounting. | Benchmark gaming, proxy exploitation, and stagnant static comparators (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| 5 | Public repositories of failed attempts | Retain failed, invalid, timed-out, and rejected attempts alongside successful runs. | Shared repositories need schemas, privacy and licensing rules, stewardship, and controls against misleading or unsafe data. | Censored and purged failed runs (@sec-data-representations-world-models). |
| 6 | University curricula and workflow review | Teach failure diagnosis, evidence qualification, matched comparison, and authority boundaries now. | A badge also needs published criteria, trained reviewers, appeals, maintenance, and evidence that the badge predicts the claimed practice. | Apprenticeship gap and erosion of structural debugging competence under routine automation (@sec-what-architect-owns). |
: **Local adoption can proceed in parallel; shared claims create dependencies.** The proposals identify work that can begin now and the infrastructure required before a team makes broader cross-organizational, silicon, or certification claims. This is a dependency map, not a program that has been run. {#tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence tbl-colwidths="[6,18,25,26,25]"}

Grand challenges and workflow badges are proposals for organizing shared research and review, rather than remedies tested in the book's worked studies. A contest could focus several groups on one unresolved problem; a badge could make the scope of a workflow review explicit. The chapter treats these two proposals as sketches whose value would need to be tested. The other four respond directly to limits encountered in the preceding chapters.

The local starting points still consume resources. Tool logs may already contain wall-clock time and accelerator hours, but license use and human triage time can require additional collection. Retaining failed runs needs storage and enough context to interpret them later. A matched baseline also spends evaluation budget. These are costs a team can plan and control; agreement on what another organization will accept is a different dependency. That distinction lets a student or a small laboratory begin a useful study without claiming that the shared infrastructure already exists.

The proposals group into four workstreams in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap. Open foundations connect tool interfaces to accessible implementation paths. Governance defines how results will be compared and disputed. Evaluation puts those rules to work in shared studies and contests. Skills and review prepare people to diagnose the resulting artifacts. These workstreams can develop concurrently, but they need to exchange records and requirements. A benchmark, for example, cannot demand a physical check that participating laboratories have no path to run.

![**Ecosystem workstreams share dependencies without imposing a universal adoption order.** Open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review exchange records and requirements. Horizontal connectors show coordination needed for cross-team claims, while local practices within every workstream begin independently. Negative design attempts feed back into schemas, checks, and surrogate calibration.](images/fig-ecosystem-roadmap){#fig-ecosystem-roadmap width="80%" fig-alt="Roadmap diagram in which four coordinating workstreams cover open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review. Actions cover schemas, physical-design paths, matched benchmarks, contests, failure repositories, curricula, and review. Dashed connectors indicate shared dependencies rather than a universal adoption sequence, and a feedback arrow returns negative attempts to the foundations."}

The defining mechanism in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap is the feedback loop returning negative design attempts to the shared foundations. Records of unroutable placements, negative timing slack, and Unified Power Format (UPF) domain violations can expose missing schema fields, benchmark constraints, or property checks and provide data for surrogate calibration. Horizontal connectors represent dependencies for cross-organizational claims, not preconditions for local exploration. Whether this coordination model scales across the semiconductor ecosystem remains an open question.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Anchor AI-Native Design Systems in Open Foundations"}
**The principle:** Develop shared interfaces, reference paths, and comparison practices around the checks that independent teams need to perform. Open schemas, accessible implementation flows, neutral benchmarks, and qualified failure repositories are proposed ways to make that work possible.

**The application:** Begin local cost, provenance, failure-retention, and comparison practices now. Require shared contracts for cross-team comparability. Support physical claims with a qualified implementation path and silicon claims with retained measurements from fabricated devices. A certification claim must state the scope actually reviewed.
:::

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

Consider what happens when a retained study record reaches another team's tool flow. A timing slack value is useful only if its units, corner, and constraint status are explicitly represented. When an optimizer exchanges spatial coordinates or power-domain declarations through ad hoc strings, a parser can accept the input while assigning it the wrong meaning. If absent measurements are encoded as zeros, a surrogate could treat an unmeasured delay or resistance as a measured zero and rank the candidate too favorably. The transfer problem of @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack therefore begins before a model makes a prediction. The organizations must agree on what the exchanged state means.

Just as Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1666 (SystemC) established common modeling semantics across commercial and open environments [@IEEE2011SystemC1666], a standards consortium (such as MLCommons[^fn-mlcommons-c12] or CHIPS Alliance) could standardize tool and record interfaces before proprietary silos lock in competing application programming interfaces (APIs). Open schema contracts would let generators, surrogate models, and verification engines interact through stable, machine-readable specifications. The proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) would formalize this coordination through three record schemas (@fig-oai-schemas).

[^fn-mlcommons-c12]: **Consortium governance in MLCommons and CHIPS Alliance**: Industry consortia such as MLCommons (which maintains MLPerf) and CHIPS Alliance define shared benchmarks, open hardware standards, and multi-stakeholder governance models [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. A dedicated Architecture Automation Working Group could adopt their submitter-auditor divisions, open rules committees, and dispute-resolution procedures to standardize closed-loop exploration benchmarks.

- **Design problem formulations.** Explicit declarations of permitted design changes, locked constraints, evaluation checks, and acceptance criteria ($s_{\text{design}}$). The prospective Lighthouse cache study (@sec-architecture-20-ontology and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces) declares one swept parameter, `l2.capacity` at 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB, against fixed cache policies and interfaces, with bank count and static random-access memory (SRAM) macro organization to be derived from capacity under a declared rule. The separate executed array study (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust) declares processing element (PE) geometries bounded at 1,024 elements with a mandatory 32 by 32 baseline. A shared schema must preserve their different status and scope. The Lighthouse prompt supplies a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) target for the compute subsystem. Its illustrative 120\ frames per second operating point corresponds to roughly 8.33\ ms per frame. A study must specify which components the power budget covers, which stages share the frame deadline, and how their execution overlaps. The array study's simulator returns alone do not establish compliance with those requirements. The formulation must also identify the technology target, distinguishing a predictive PDK such as ASAP7 from commercial signoff on a node such as TSMC N3E. When a generator proposes a different hardware or software organization, the formulation must describe the changed interfaces and obligations so the receiving team can determine which earlier checks still apply.
- **Lineage headers.** Declarations of candidate artifacts, parent inputs, transformations, tool flags, structural representations, and environment configurations ($s_{\text{env}}$). A cryptographic hash identifies exact bytes; an authenticated Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) attestation binds an issuer to a declaration [@SLSA2026Framework].[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12] Neither mechanism proves semantic correctness, and an attestation remains only as trustworthy as its builder, signing key, and storage path. Lineage headers track the exact inputs and environments used to generate an artifact, such as a SystemC memory controller or a high-level synthesis kernel (@sec-data-representations-world-models). Rather than relying on informal logs, these headers retain structured records of prompt and commit hashes, intermediate representations (IR) (like abstract syntax trees (ASTs), control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) / Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT)), execution seeds, and environment definitions (container digests and CLI arguments). A team might export structural hashes, compiler pass fingerprints, and bounding-box geometry metrics while withholding internal transistor topologies, unreleased instruction set architecture (ISA) opcodes, and proprietary foundry cell libraries. Those summaries still require disclosure review, including an assessment of what several records reveal together.
- **Multi-fidelity environmental contracts and tool programmatic qualification.** Typed input prerequisites, output schemas, declared error assumptions, status semantics, and property-appropriate checks across analytical models, cycle-level simulators, and register-transfer level (RTL) tools. Assessments verify whether tools such as gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA expose pinned container interfaces, structured state exports, checkpoint behavior, machine-parsable failures, and documented checks (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) state properties that bounded model checking (BMC) can check within a declared execution bound and under stated assumptions.[^fn-bmc-c12] A passing bounded check needs a separate completeness argument to establish the property for all executions of the model, and still cannot exclude a deadlock or other behavior the model omits.

[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12]: **Software supply chain attestations and SLSA**: Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) provides machine-readable specifications for artifact build provenance. While SLSA Build Level 1 provenance can remain unsigned, higher levels require cryptographically authenticated provenance [@SLSA2026Framework]. A cryptographic signature authenticates the identity of the builder and execution environment, but it does not verify semantic circuit correctness.

[^fn-bmc-c12]: **Bounded model checking and completeness thresholds**: Bounded model checking (BMC) searches circuit executions up to a finite depth ($k$ cycles) for counterexamples to an encoded property [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Passing that bound alone does not establish unbounded correctness. For a finite-state model, a sufficiently large bound can establish the property if a completeness threshold or recurrence diameter for that specific model and property has been formally justified.

![**The proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) would standardize three classes of record.** Design Problem Formulations declare search bounds and obligations; Attempt Lineage Headers identify artifacts and signed transformation declarations; Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contracts declare tool interfaces, assumptions, statuses, and checks. Together they support selective cross-organizational exchange, subject to separate access control, confidentiality, and trust policies.](images/fig-oai-schemas){#fig-oai-schemas width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of three proposed Open Agentic Interface records: design problem formulation, attempt lineage header, and environmental contract. They capture bounds, artifact identities, transformation declarations, input prerequisites, error assumptions, and tool checks. A bottom box represents selective cross-organizational exchange subject to separate trust and confidentiality controls."}

Serialization is an implementation choice rather than the contract. Protocol Buffers provide typed message definitions and cross-language serialization, while JSON-LD (a linked data format for JSON) connects execution records to shared vocabularies through persistent identifiers. Neither format settles the meaning of a tool result. An Open Agentic Interface lineage header serializes run identifiers, parent hashes, tool flags, container digests, and artifact hashes to record transformation provenance. A receiving tool uses this header to locate an implementation artifact, such as a static timing report, and verify that its bytes match the declared hash. Before consuming the report, it checks the enclosing record's schema version, slack units, and status; missing measurements must not default to zero slack. If an attestation accompanies the record, a valid signature identifies the issuer of that declaration; it does not establish that the timing constraints were correct. The header supplies identity and dependencies, while the environmental contract supplies the interpretation rules.


Where CIRCT and MLIR standardize the structural syntax of hardware modules and compiler dialects, OAI would carry the orchestration, lineage, and verification metadata governing how tools and generators manipulate those representations. It would also sit beside the interchange formats the industry already runs on, LEF/DEF for physical geometry, IEEE 1801 UPF for power intent, OpenAccess[^fn-openaccess-c12] for design databases, and FIRRTL for generator output, carrying the record of how a run used those artifacts rather than replacing any of them. Each record class has a different preservation requirement. Problem formulations must retain their meaning after external parsing, lineage headers must remain interpretable apart from the original execution, and environmental contracts must make changes in tool behavior explicit when a tool is updated.

[^fn-openaccess-c12]: **OpenAccess design database standard**: An industry-standard binary database and application programming interface managed by the Silicon Integration Initiative (Si2) for representing integrated circuit design objects, hierarchy, and physical connectivity across EDA tools. High-level workflow schemas complement OpenAccess by standardizing orchestration, attempt lineage, and property assertions across tools rather than managing in-memory physical geometries.

An interface proposal would become more useful if design teams required compatible exports from the tools they procure and contributed tests for how those exports are interpreted. That shared demand could reduce repeated wrapper work and let teams compare tool behavior on the same inputs. The consortium would still have to maintain compatibility tests as tools and schemas change.

## Precompetitive Open Infrastructure and Shared Tooling {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

In deep-submicron and nanoscale fabrication, routing congestion, power-grid IR drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c12] UPF power-domain isolation, thermal dissipation, and manufacturability demand implementation evidence calibrated to the target node. Device structures, manufacturing rules, and interconnect resistance and capacitance[^fn-rc-parasitics-c12] vary with the process. Their effect on timing depends on the placed and routed design, so a nominal node label cannot establish that a candidate will close timing. Because commercial foundries protect their intellectual property behind strict nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), proprietary signoff tools, and qualified design-rule manuals, academic laboratories and early-stage startups face a structural barrier to physical design exploration.[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]

[^fn-ir-drop-c12]: **Static and dynamic voltage droop**: Voltage degradation across the power distribution network arises from static resistive loss ($V = I \times R$) through metal grids and dynamic inductive droop ($V = L \cdot di/dt$) during simultaneous clock-edge switching surges. Localized dynamic droop degrades gate switching speeds and introduces transient timing violations that nominal static timing analysis fails to capture.

[^fn-rc-parasitics-c12]: **Nanoscale interconnect parasitics**: At advanced semiconductor nodes (7\ nm and below), wire cross-sections shrink and copper barrier scattering increases interconnect resistivity exponentially. Signal propagation delay through on-chip wire resistance ($R$) and parasitic capacitance ($C$) dominates gate delay, requiring macro placers and routers to optimize for layer-dependent wire characteristics rather than planar wirelength alone.

[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]: **Proprietary isolation in physical design kits**: Foundry access agreements and disclosure restrictions limit which researchers can rerun an implementation study or inspect its design-rule assumptions. Review by another authorized industrial team may still be possible, but it remains distinct from open scientific reproduction.

Expanding open-source physical-design infrastructure and multi-project wafer (MPW) shuttle access narrows this structural divide. Open process design kits (PDKs), including SkyWater SKY130 (130\ nm CMOS) [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], IHP SG13G2 (130\ nm BiCMOS), and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (180\ nm), expose models, libraries, and design rules for research on manufacturable processes. A manufacturable target process does not make every open PDK release production-qualified; fabrication requires a release and checks accepted by the chosen service [@IHPOpenPDK; @GlobalFoundriesGF180MCUOpenPDK]. Coupled with the open-source intermediate representation (IR) infrastructure of the CIRCT/Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) compiler ecosystem [@CIRCT] and open EDA engines (OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA), open PDKs let researchers inspect and version more of the implementation flow. Reproducing a particular result still requires its inputs, tool versions, constraints, and execution record; open availability alone does not supply those dependencies.

Reusing established synthesis, layout, and simulation infrastructure lets a design team concentrate effort on candidate microarchitectures and constraint formulations rather than re-implementing foundational toolchains. However, the standard-library analogy concerns reuse, not inherited correctness. A generated macro still requires rigorous signoff checks in its concrete integration context, even if its upstream toolchain and neighboring IP blocks have been exercised in prior tapeouts. Shared open-source dependencies make verification environments easier to reproduce; they do not render new compositions pre-verified.



In academic research, ASAP7 serves as a predictive 7\ nm PDK for modeling scaling trends rather than manufacturable signoff [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12] It includes device models, design rules, and extraction decks, but its resulting designs are not manufacturable. Its modeled power, performance, and area (PPA) therefore cannot substitute for signoff against a commercial process's qualified decks. A candidate architecture that ranks highly under ASAP7 may fail timing or routing constraints when subjected to commercial foundry design rules. Correlating predictive-PDK evaluations with commercial TSMC N7, N3, or N2 characteristics constitutes a distinct research claim requiring matched industrial baselines, documented modeling assumptions, and an assessment of the differences between predicted and reference results.

[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12]: **Predictive process design kits**: A collection of device models and design rules developed to model projected physical scaling trends rather than support manufacturing on a qualified commercial line. The 7\ nm ASAP7 library provides an openly accessible academic example [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].

## Silicon Shuttles and Cost Reduction {#sec-silicon-shuttles}

Timing, power delivery, and thermal behavior can be analyzed before fabrication, but each analysis depends on its device models, parasitics, operating conditions, and package assumptions. A predictive kit supports claims within that modeled environment. Foundry-qualified analysis supports a different implementation claim, and empirical validation requires measurements on a fabricated die. The unmeasured checks in @sec-what-architect-owns therefore call for a named implementation or measurement path, not an undifferentiated demand for silicon. Shuttles address the final step by sharing fabrication costs among research designs, extending the MPC79 and MOSIS precedent [@Conway1981MPCAdventures; @MOSIS1981VLSI]. The cost comparison in @fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse explains why that access matters.

![**Fabrication access spans different processes and submission sizes.** (a) Compiled costs compare full-reticle masks, commercial MPW prototypes, and open-shuttle tiles. Mask-set values range from $\$35\ \text{thousand}$ ($2\ \mu\text{m}$) to $\$48\ \text{million}$ (3\ nm). The $\$460\ \text{thousand}$ prototype and $\$50$ open-process tile offer different capabilities, not a price reduction for the same chip. Shared fabrication follows MOSIS [@MOSIS1981VLSI]. (b) The Tiny Tapeout snapshot counts $152\to 4{,}026$ submissions across 22 shuttles. These record participation, not completed silicon validation; open PDKs support the implementation path [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK].](images/fig-shuttle-cost-democratization){#fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse width="80%" fig-alt="Dual-panel illustration comparing mask-set, commercial prototype, and open-shuttle entry costs across different processes and submission sizes, alongside Tiny Tapeout submission counts. The retained snapshot reaches 4,026 cumulative submissions; these are not counts of verified silicon designs."}

The educational opportunity in @fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse is access to a smaller, different experiment. Full-reticle mask sets at advanced process nodes require tens of millions of dollars in tooling capital,[^fn-mask-costs-c12] while a multiplexed tile on an open process[^fn-tinytapeout-architecture-c12] cannot reproduce the capacity or physical conditions of a leading-edge commercial prototype. Fabricating on mature planar nodes (such as 130\ nm or 180\ nm) enables functional bringup, educational verification, and basic post-silicon measurement, but it cannot validate sub-5nm physical closure challenges such as fin-pitch routing congestion, extreme dynamic $IR$-drop transients, thermo-mechanical package warping, or multi-gigahertz clock distribution. It can still let students bring up a fabricated design, compare measurements with predictions, and investigate discrepancies. Likewise, the submission growth in panel (b) records participation in that path; it does not establish that every submitted design was fabricated, delivered, or successfully measured. The architecture question must fit the process, area, interfaces, and observability the shuttle actually provides.

[^fn-mask-costs-c12]: **Photolithographic mask tooling and respin economics**: Advanced process nodes utilizing extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography require dozens of optical reticles, with optical proximity correction and multi-patterning driving mask-set tooling costs past $\$40\ \text{million}$. A functional or physical defect escaping signoff requires fabricating a revised mask set (a silicon respin), imposing months of foundry delay and millions of dollars in unrecoverable non-recurring engineering capital.

[^fn-tinytapeout-architecture-c12]: **Multiplexed open-shuttle tiles**: Educational shuttles achieve substantial cost reductions by tiling hundreds of independent digital designs onto a single shared silicon die. A centralized digital multiplexer routes power, clocks, and I/O pins to one selected design at a time, restricting submissions to low frequencies (tens of megahertz), small standard-cell counts, and digital-only interfaces without dedicated high-speed pads.

Tiny Tapeout's public run catalog and Europractice's MPW service illustrate different routes to shared fabrication [@TinyTapeoutRunCatalog; @EuropracticeMPWPrototyping]. Google's 2022 announcement of OpenMPW runs with Efabless provides an earlier example [@Google2022OpenMPW]. These programs differ in submission interfaces, process access, and implementation requirements; a team must check the terms and accepted PDK release for its planned run. The proposed extension for automatically generated macros is shared characterization infrastructure. A research shuttle could allocate isolated power-monitored rails, ring oscillators and on-chip transient voltage droop monitors for timing and power-delivery characterization across voltage and temperature,[^fn-ring-oscillators-c12] and JTAG interfaces for collecting telemetry. Those features would have to be designed into the vehicle and qualified; they are not implied by booking space on a shared wafer.

[^fn-ring-oscillators-c12]: **On-chip ring oscillators and droop monitors for silicon characterization**: An on-chip test structure consisting of an odd number of inverting logic gates in a closed feedback loop whose natural oscillation frequency directly reflects stage gate delay. Fabricating arrays of ring oscillators and localized high-bandwidth voltage droop detectors across varying cell types, metal layers, and supply rails allows characterization teams to measure true local gate delay, dynamic $IR$-drop transients, and intra-die process variation across voltage and temperature, providing ground-truth measurements to calibrate multi-fidelity timing and power models.

A retained measurement campaign could then connect each fabricated candidate to its timing and power observations and to the models that predicted them. Yield claims would additionally need an appropriate population of devices and test conditions. This would give the community a path to calibrating surrogates against silicon rather than only against another tool. Containerized open flows improve repeatability, but do not grant commercial-tool rights or close the gap to a different foundry process.[^fn-eda-eula-restrictions-c12]

[^fn-eda-eula-restrictions-c12]: **Commercial EDA licensing restrictions and closed data models**: Commercial electronic design automation licenses contain strict end-user agreement clauses prohibiting third-party benchmarking, reverse engineering, and publishing comparative runtime or PPA figures without explicit vendor authorization. Furthermore, proprietary binary databases (such as vendor-specific OpenAccess extensions and closed timing graph representations) lack open programmatic APIs, forcing automated agentic workflows into brittle tool-control wrappers that complicate reproducible interaction and headless cloud orchestration.

## Consortium Governance and Benchmarking {#sec-neutral-governance}

Access to an implementation flow lets a team produce physical evidence, but comparison across teams also requires agreement on the experiment. If groups choose different RTL blocks, leave compute hours uncounted, or tune prompts against their evaluation tasks, a reported margin can mix architectural improvement with unequal budgets and selection effects, including the optimizer's curse (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). Shared tasks, reference comparators, disclosure rules, and audit procedures would address the benchmark-health risks analyzed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect.

Drawing on the governance model of MLCommons[^fn-mlcommons-c12] and MLPerf [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf], an independent Architecture Automation Working Group under an established body (such as MLCommons,[^fn-mlcommons-c12] Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation (SPEC), CHIPS Alliance, or IEEE Council on Electronic Design Automation (CEDA)) could maintain these shared rules and hear disputes over results. Separate divisions would let researchers pursue different kinds of comparison while making resource budgets explicit. Method attribution would still require the controlled comparisons and ablations developed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. Such a working group would take on three mandates:

- **Reference problem suites.** Problem suites grounded in realistic industrial constraints, spanning 3\ W mobile extended-reality (XR) spatial processing, RISC-V RV64GCV vector clusters, datacenter tensor acceleration, Compute Express Link (CXL) memory expansion, and Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) chiplet interconnect management. While digital controller logic, packet arbiters, and link-layer state machines can be explored and synthesized using open automated flows, physical layer (PHY) analog front-ends (including high-speed serializer/deserializer circuits, phase-locked loops, and calibrated impedance terminators) remain proprietary, foundry-specific analog macros that require dedicated mixed-signal signoff. Each suite would need maintainers for its reference implementations and tool configurations, versioned releases, and a rule for deciding when a correction requires results to be rerun. Otherwise, a reported gain could reflect a weak or outdated comparator.
- **Closed and open benchmark divisions.** A Closed Division where entrants compete under locked tool wrappers, fixed compute budgets, and identical baseline matching to compare search methods within those conditions. An Open Division could permit custom search procedures, heuristics, or proprietary surrogates while retaining the task's architectural requirements and disclosing multi-dimensional workflow costs and artifact lineage. Its results would compare complete approaches under the declared conditions.
- **Total workflow-cost accounting.** Mandatory accounting for the multi-dimensional resource vector ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), including GPU compute hours, EDA license checkout minutes, and human triage time.

Neutrality would also depend on how contested results are handled. Before accepting submissions, the working group would need to specify what evidence a challenge must supply, how reviewers with conflicts of interest are excluded, and when a disputed run must be reproduced, corrected, or withdrawn. Published decisions could then explain how the rules were applied, so that comparable disputes receive comparable treatment.

Together the three mandates would give research groups a common basis for comparison. A contest would also need to state which constraints its score captures and which remain untested, since a gain on the contest's metric may fail to transfer to other design tasks.[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]

[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]: **Overfitting in competitive benchmarks**: An optimization method can improve scores on a fixed benchmark suite without generalizing to real-world industrial circuit designs. Evaluators must distinguish performance gains on the declared challenge from verified transfer to production workloads.

## Grand Challenges and Design Contests {#sec-grand-challenges}

Where consortium governance would establish neutral baseline rules and cost accounting, competitive grand challenges apply that framework to focus research on unresolved architectural bottlenecks. Shared traces and evaluation rules have supported comparisons in branch prediction through Championship Branch Prediction (CBP) [@CBP2016BranchPrediction], and data prefetching through Data Prefetching Championship (DPC) [@DPC2015DataPrefetching]. ChampSim provides a simulation platform used in architecture research, education, and competitions [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim]. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Grand Challenges in autonomous vehicles [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley] and ImageNet in computer vision [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet] offer related examples of shared evaluation tasks. EDA already has a history of shared design contests. [ISPD's contest archive](https://www.ispd.cc/contests/08/) includes placement in 2005 and global routing in 2007 and 2008; the [CAD Contest at ICCAD](https://www.iccad-contest.org/) began in 2012. An Architecture 2.0 challenge could be a track alongside existing contests rather than a new institution. Three such tracks are sketched below.

- **Constrained physical PPA generation.** RTL carried through a named implementation flow from a high-level specification under a declared power and thermal envelope. Entrants would be judged on the declared physical checks and intervention budget; passing the contest would not authorize tapeout.
- **Sample-efficient design-space exploration.** Microarchitectural configurations for heterogeneous workloads under a fixed simulation budget. Entrants would return candidates nondominated among those evaluated; no evaluated design is at least as good on every objective and better on one. A possible score is the fraction of evaluator-declared objective targets reached within the budget. For an energy–latency target, at least one returned candidate must meet both bounds and all feasibility checks. Targets would be fixed before submissions, and the score would not imply that the global Pareto frontier had been found.
- **Adversarial red-teaming and hardware security.** Detection of seeded timing exceptions, malicious logic, and verification loopholes in generated collateral. Timing exceptions would require constraint audits and appropriate timing analysis; SVA and BMC could expose encoded functional violations within a declared model and bound. A possible score would count correctly detected seeded defects while recording false alarms and the checks used. It would establish coverage of the declared challenge set, not the absence of every possible Trojan or timing defect.

The unsuccessful entries can remain useful after the winning score is superseded. Their retained inputs and diagnostic returns show which candidates failed under the contest's conditions, providing material for the repository proposed next.

## Public Repositories of Failed Runs {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

Discarding failed runs censors the data available to learned surrogates (@sec-data-representations-world-models). A team may treat a failed synthesis or place-and-route run as a broken experiment and remove its log. Yet an unroutable floorplan or a reported timing violation can reveal a feasibility limit that a corpus of successful designs never shows. Training only on the survivors leaves that part of the design space poorly represented.[^fn-survivorship-bias-c12] Retaining negative results gives later studies observations near those limits, provided contributors distinguish a design failure from a tool crash or configuration error. A failed attempt records what happened under particular constraints, tool settings, and resource limits; it does not by itself establish that the design is infeasible. A consortium repository would need three forms of support to make these runs reusable.

[^fn-survivorship-bias-c12]: **Survivorship bias in surrogate training data**: Training predictive surrogate models solely on successful, design-rule-clean, and timing-closed implementations creates a truncated sample that excludes the failure boundaries of the physical design space. Without exposure to unroutable floorplans and severe timing violations, surrogates cannot learn the non-linear cliffs characterizing real EDA constraints.

- **Execution traces and run context.** Complete command-line interface (CLI) logs, tool return codes, standard error (stderr) streams, and resource consumption telemetry for failed synthesis, simulation, and place-and-route passes. Each record would also need to identify its inputs, constraints, tool and PDK versions, dependencies, seeds where applicable, and execution budget. Records with unavailable dependencies could still support diagnosis, but should state what another team cannot reproduce.
- **Qualified failure annotations.** Timing violations (worst negative slack $\text{WNS} < 0$),[^fn-wns-tns-c12] design rule check (DRC) geometry violations, assertion counterexamples, deadlock states, and routing failures with congestion maps are observations from a run. A shared taxonomy should distinguish them from infrastructure failures such as license timeouts. An annotation should separate the observed symptom from a suspected or confirmed root cause and identify the supporting diagnostic evidence. A license timeout supplies no feasibility label for the candidate; a timing violation describes the evaluated implementation under its recorded constraints.
- **Disclosure review and filtering.** Proposed sanitization pipelines could convert proprietary physical netlists into normalized graph embeddings, anonymized congestion heatmaps, and relative slack distributions, stripping absolute die coordinates, foundry cell-type names, and top-level block pinouts. These transformations would still need disclosure review because patterns across several failed runs may expose information that no single record reveals. The released record should also state which diagnostic information the transformation removes, so users can judge which interpretations remain supported.

[^fn-wns-tns-c12]: **Worst negative slack and total negative slack**: In static timing analysis, worst negative slack (WNS) measures the timing delay violation on the single most critical endpoint in the design, determining whether the clock frequency target is met. Total negative slack (TNS) sums the negative slack across all violating endpoints; a design with minor WNS but massive TNS indicates pervasive structural congestion or clock-tree failure rather than an isolated local path delay.

Publishing qualified negative data can help other teams avoid known dead ends and supply observations near the feasibility boundaries used to calibrate multi-fidelity surrogates. OpenROAD-flow-scripts already makes public test results, logs, and artifacts for reproducing failures available through its [continuous integration infrastructure](https://openroad-flow-scripts.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contrib/CI.html). The proposed repository would add shared annotations and disclosure practices so that contributors could reuse failures across different projects and tool flows. Maintaining the repository would also require people to preserve tool dependencies, review annotations, and track whether old runs remain interpretable.[^fn-abandonware-c12] A team can begin by retaining this run context and separating observed outcomes from causal diagnoses in its own records; shared taxonomy maintenance and public disclosure review require coordination across contributors. Contributors would need to assess what the accumulated records reveal about a product's design space, a disclosure question taken up in @sec-ecosystem-open-questions.

[^fn-abandonware-c12]: **Software degradation and infrastructure rot**: Rapid drift in upstream open-source EDA dependencies, Linux kernel libraries, container base images, and external web APIs can render published hardware design flows unreproducible within months. Long-term workflow preservation requires hermetic container digests, pinned tool binaries, and dedicated active stewardship rather than static code archives.

## Sustaining Research and Industrial Adoption {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

If shared foundations made closed-loop exploration economical at industry scale, problem formulation, signoff review, and cross-layer trade-offs could account for more of the remaining work. Repeated automated execution could also create demand for different EDA licensing arrangements, shifting from seat-bound annual floating licenses toward metered, cloud-native burst capacity aligned with autonomous sweep surges.[^fn-eda-licensing-c12] Lower front-end labor costs might make smaller-volume application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) viable for regional laboratories and startups, although masks, packaging, and physical validation would still have to fit the budget. These are possible consequences of the proposed infrastructure, not results established here. Their value would depend in part on whether engineers retained the diagnostic skills needed to evaluate the resulting designs.

[^fn-eda-licensing-c12]: **EDA burst licensing and commercial friction**: Commercial electronic design automation tools historically rely on annual term licenses or floating network FlexLM tokens priced for human design teams. Autonomous closed-loop exploration generates massive burst demands, requiring hundreds of parallel tool instances for brief optimization sweeps followed by idle evaluation intervals. Cloud-based consumption licensing remains an active commercial friction; vendor end-user agreements, site-locked daemon restrictions, and container startup latency continue to impede elastic automated scaling.

## Curriculum and Diagnostic Competence {#sec-curriculum-certification}

The shared records, implementation paths, and failure repositories above would also change what students can practice. RTL construction and point-tool execution remain useful ways to learn hardware behavior. A curriculum for AI-native design systems must connect that experience to formulating requirements, building evaluators, orchestrating tool runs, and diagnosing generated artifacts. Four areas of competence organize that extension:

- **Specification engineering across requirement domains.** Expressing functional, timing, power, and interface requirements in forms that can be checked across the hardware–software stack.
- **Verification of generated designs.** Developing testbench architectures, property-appropriate checks, and adversarial red-teaming methodologies.
- **Search space formulation.** Defining evaluator-driven search spaces, constraint boundaries, and Pareto trade-off synthesis.
- **Heterogeneous system integration.** Integrating domain-specific accelerators across CPU, neural processing unit (NPU), memory, and packaging boundaries.

The educational risk is the apprenticeship gap identified in @sec-what-architect-owns. If automation removes routine debugging from a junior engineer's work, a curriculum must supply another way to learn what a timing report, waveform, or congestion map means. Otherwise the organization may assign responsibility without the experience needed to exercise it, the problem examined in @sec-sustaining-responsibility [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. Bainbridge's analysis explains why additional automation does not by itself resolve this gap [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

::: {.callout-law title="Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation in Hardware Design"}
**The Classical Principle:** Automating routine tasks can reduce opportunities to maintain the skills needed when the operator must take over. The remaining faults may demand more experience precisely when routine practice has diminished [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

**Hardware Design Application:** A summary score can report that a candidate failed without teaching the reviewer how to distinguish a layout problem from an incorrect timing constraint. Training must include the underlying artifacts and the checks that separate those causes.

**Mitigation Strategy:** Implement shadow verification audits and diagnostic fault-injection training to restore the operator's exposure to structural debugging without reverting to routine manual drafting (@sec-law-ironies-automation in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

Two laboratory practices can provide that experience in a setting where mistakes can be investigated before fabrication. In a shadow verification audit, a student follows an automated exploration run, forms an independent hypothesis about the bottleneck the optimizer is pursuing, and audits the generated RTL and its Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) declarations. The student then compares that diagnosis with the instructor's review. The learning comes from explaining why a reported improvement survives or fails the checks, not merely observing the run complete.

In a fault-injection laboratory, instructors seed a candidate with a clock-domain crossing (CDC) synchronization defect,[^fn-cdc-metastability-c12] an unhandled finite state machine (FSM) reset state, or a silent false path in its SDC constraints.[^fn-sdc-false-path-c12] Students select the appropriate evidence for each defect: structural CDC checks for unsafe crossings, simulation or formal properties for reset behavior, and timing-constraint audits for the false path. Ordinary RTL simulation does not model analog metastability, and a passing functional trace does not validate a timing exception (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Explaining those observation limits is part of the exercise. Shared repositories of failed runs could supply additional cases with retained inputs and instructor-checked diagnoses.

[^fn-cdc-metastability-c12]: **Clock-domain crossing metastability**: When an asynchronous signal transitions within the setup and hold aperture of a receiving flip-flop, the register output can hover at an indeterminate intermediate voltage for an unpredictable duration [@Cummings2008CDC]. Standard digital RTL simulators resolve setup and hold violations instantaneously to discrete binary values ($0$ or $1$), completely obscuring downstream synchronization failures that manifest as intermittent hardware crashes in fabricated silicon.

[^fn-sdc-false-path-c12]: **Static timing false-path declarations**: A timing constraint declared via `set_false_path` in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) instructs static timing analysis tools to ignore signal propagation delays along specified paths. Declaring a false path on a path that is physically and logically exercisable silences real timing violations, causing synthesis and layout tools to under-buffer the path and producing defective silicon that fails at operating speed.

Where commercial-tool access is available, students can also compare OpenROAD and Yosys reports with corresponding industrial signoff reports, identifying which quantities and assumptions transfer. A semester-long course can follow the four parts of this book, moving from the design question through representations, methods, environments, and feedback, then into execution, transfer, evaluation, ownership, and shared infrastructure. The design principles established across the chapters provide an exit test; students should be able to apply them to a problem the course never assigned. The companion site carries the week-by-week version, since a syllabus dates faster than a chapter.

Instructors can begin these exercises without a shared certification scheme. Published research raises a separate coordination problem: readers need to know which parts of an automated workflow received independent review. Conference artifact evaluation committees at venues such as the International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO), Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS), and Design Automation Conference (DAC) could pilot an Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badge grounded in computational reproducibility practice [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].[^fn-awc-badge-c12] ACM's artifact badging already distinguishes an artifact that is available from one that has been evaluated and one whose results were reproduced; a proposed AWC badge could build on those distinctions to report workflow checks discussed in this book. These include replay under declared execution conditions, signed lineage, total-cost accounting, surrogate calibration against signoff checks, and physical closure on an open manufacturable kit.

The proposed badge would need to name exactly what reviewers checked. Computational repeatability and lineage could be assessed for a simulator study; surrogate calibration would require a declared reference; an implementation study could additionally be reviewed for physical closure in a named open flow. These are different scopes, and a badge should not imply that each artifact passed all of them. Even open-flow physical closure would not establish commercial foundry signoff, electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection, process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) yield qualification, or packaging thermo-mechanical qualification. Nor would computational review substitute for measurements on fabricated silicon or authorize commercial tapeout. Publishing the reviewed scope would let readers use the badge as evidence of specific checks rather than as a general certificate of architectural correctness.

[^fn-awc-badge-c12]: **Autonomous Workflow Certified badge**: A proposed designation in this chapter, extending computational reproducibility principles to an explicitly scoped review of an automated design workflow. The cited work motivates reproducibility practice; it does not establish this badge [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

The questions that close each chapter state what its argument could not settle. Here the unresolved issues concern arrangements between teams. They ask how shared infrastructure could support comparisons while preserving access, independence, and confidentiality.

- **When do architectural rankings from open predictive PDKs survive commercial signoff?** A predictive kit such as ASAP7 supports comparisons within its modeled process, but those rankings do not establish how candidates compare under a commercial foundry's rules and models. The shared infrastructure would need a way to discover which constraints cause rankings to change without requiring every contributor to obtain the same restricted access. The unresolved issue is how matched open and commercial evaluations could establish useful transfer limits while respecting the foundry's disclosure restrictions.

- **How can a neutral evaluation consortium remain independent when its rulings disqualify member products?** Members may supply both the funding and the expertise needed to evaluate a result, yet face a commercial loss when an audit rejects it. An evaluation audit that invalidates a marquee product claim risks prompt retaliation through withdrawn compute grants, steering-committee boycotts, or revoked tool licenses. Publishing rules makes the decision inspectable, but does not settle how the consortium sustains its reviewers, funding, and enforcement under that pressure. Possible arrangements include public support, audits distributed among competing groups, or structural firewalls separating benchmark governance from commercial tool vendors; their ability to preserve both technical competence and independence would need to be tested.

- **How much of a product's design space does a corpus of its failed runs reveal?** Removing coordinates, cell names, and pinouts does not establish that disclosure is safe. A failure corpus also records which floorplans a team tried and abandoned, at what congestion and under what slack. The combination may reveal information absent from individual records. The proposed repository therefore needs an evaluation of reconstruction risk and of whether contribution pooling, bounded release under a privacy budget, or delayed release after product launch would reduce that risk to a level contributors can accept.

- **Who can sustain historical reference tasks and reruns across institutions?** The benchmark-renewal methods discussed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect depend on continued access to reference tasks, earlier systems, and the tools needed to rerun them. A distributed archive could outlast a single laboratory, but preserving a package does not preserve its licenses, services, or compatible execution environment. Proprietary cloud APIs, closed tool binaries, and expiring foundry nondisclosure agreements create digital rot that can render reference benchmarks unexecutable within two to three years. The open issue is which shared custody and containerized archiving arrangements could keep historical comparisons usable as institutions and vendors change, and how to state the limits when some dependencies can no longer be recovered.

- **How can independent groups test the integrity of a consortium's reference baselines?** Shared reference flows and audit scripts can drift or favor some candidates, so agreement to use them does not establish that they remain credible comparators. Cryptographically signed lineage can reveal which artifacts were used; it cannot establish that the comparator was configured competently or given a fair budget. Independent reruns and adversarial re-audits could challenge that technical basis, but the community still needs to determine what access and coverage make such challenges effective.

## Summary and Immediate Action Items {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

The fabrication-access story that opens this chapter joins two kinds of work: methods that a team can learn and shared services that let it test what it builds. The proposed ecosystem needs the same connection. A record format has value when another laboratory can interpret it; a reference flow has value when researchers can reach the checks their claims require. Individual teams can begin preparing those contributions while the broader agreements are still being formed.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Prepare records for another reader.** Retain units, versions, status meanings, costs, and dependencies so a collaborator can interpret a run without relying on its author's memory.
- **Keep failures with their context.** Preserve inputs and diagnostic returns, distinguish tool failures from rejected designs, and review disclosure risks before contributing records to a shared repository.
- **Name the implementation path.** Identify which modeled checks your open flow supports and what additional process access or fabricated measurements a broader claim would require.
- **Make a comparison reusable.** Version the task, comparator, checks, and workflow costs together so another group can attempt the same comparison and report where it differs.
- **Teach diagnosis through retained artifacts.** Use shadow audits and fault-injection exercises to let students explain failures, select checks, and recognize what those checks cannot observe.
:::

The questions across this book are food for thought, not a complete research agenda. They leave room for a student to contribute before the discipline has settled these arrangements. A new study may reveal that two tools disagree about a status, that a shared benchmark omits a relevant constraint, or that an apparently anonymous failure record exposes too much. State your own question, identify the observation that could answer it, and retain what the study leaves unresolved. Carry that habit to the next workload, tool, or implementation process, including those this lecture could not anticipate.
